title: Finance: Household Resilience to Audited Financial Analysis

stageOutcomes.outcome: Explain a household's cash, debt, insurance and time-value trade-offs using stated assumptions.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A synthetic household plan with amortization, inflation-adjusted goals and a loss-of-income scenario.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Reconcile financial statements and compare investments by cash flows, diversification, costs and suitability constraints.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A linked statement/ratio analysis and a fictional investment policy with a cost-aware rebalancing worksheet.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Evaluate corporate projects and valuation ranges under financing, macroeconomic and modelling uncertainty.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A capital-budgeting decision, enterprise-to-equity bridge and scenario-sensitive valuation model.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Build, audit and explain a decision-ready financial model without disguising assumptions as facts.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A versioned household/corporate analysis dossier, independent error challenge and bounded decision memo.

resources.title: RBI: FAME financial awareness messages
resources.license: Official public education; no redistribution permission asserted
resources.notes: Official index links the fourth-edition booklet: Financial Competencies, Basic Banking, Digital Financial Literacy and Consumer Protection. Open the named English material on demand; the app does not mirror it. No bank account is required.

resources.title: RBI financial education: Money Kumar
resources.notes: RBI's FAME page identifies this series as explaining the Reserve Bank's role and functions. Select English on the language page. Illustrations are historical; verify current policy statements separately and do not infer current rates.

resources.title: Varsity: Personal Finance - Insurance
resources.notes: Introduction explains health-policy conditions and exclusions; chapters also address incentives. Commercial contributors and linked services can have conflicts. Ignore purchase prompts, historical numerical claims and product recommendations; use a fictional policy.

resources.title: Varsity: Fundamental Analysis
resources.notes: Verified chapters cover annual reports, P&L, balance sheets, cash flow, ratios and DCF. Use statement mechanics with invented companies. Historical company examples are not current prices, accounting advice or recommendations.

resources.title: Varsity: Integrated Financial Modelling
resources.notes: Verified chapters include workbook setup, assumptions, revenue/asset/debt schedules, projections, cash flow, FCFF/FCFE, WACC and DCF. Implement an original workbook in free LibreOffice or Python; Microsoft Excel and example downloads are not required.

resources.title: RBI: Basic Financial Literacy
resources.license: Officially linked public recording; no redistribution permission asserted
resources.notes: Exact recording linked as Basic Financial Literacy on RBI's FAME page. Playback may require regional/consent access; the FAME reading is the free text alternative. Do not infer current financial-product terms from the video.

resources.title: MIT 15.401 Finance Theory I: Present Value Relations
resources.license: MIT OCW covered material: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; third-party exceptions apply
resources.notes: Official lecture topic page verified from the course index. Use discounting and cash-flow timing theory, not historical market yields or US legal/account examples as Indian rules.

resources.title: NYU Stern: Damodaran valuation and tools webcasts
resources.notes: Free webcasts; no textbook purchase required. Verified tools include From financial disclosures to value, Terminal Value Check, and EV, Firm Value and Equity Value. Historical filings, lease treatments and numerical inputs need current-context checks. Do not download/rehost examples as app content.

modules.title: 01. Household cash flow and debt
modules.description: Use a fictional household to separate cash availability, net worth and borrowing cost.

lessons.title: Build a cash-flow budget and resilience buffer
objectives: Classify income, essentials, discretionary costs and irregular obligations.
Distinguish a monthly surplus from liquid emergency capacity.

topics.title: Household statements
details: Net worth is assets minus liabilities at a date.
A budget is a flow plan; illiquid assets cannot pay every immediate bill.

topics.title: Resilience
details: Annual bills need explicit sinking-fund treatment.
An emergency target depends on obligations and income uncertainty, not a universal number.

video.locator: Basic Financial Literacy recording linked by RBI: budgeting, saving and responsible financial decisions. Use the FAME reading if playback is unavailable.

reading.locator: Open the fourth-edition FAME booklet, Financial Competencies theme: use budgeting and saving messages to distinguish cash planning from product selection.

assignment.title: A fictional household cash map
instructions: Use invented monthly income INR 40000, essentials 22000, discretionary spending 6000, debt payment 5000 and annual bills 24000.
Allocate the annual bills monthly and calculate free surplus without recording any real account information.
Compare a one-month income interruption with a three-month interruption and propose a justified hypothetical liquidity target.
acceptanceCriteria: Annual bills reserve INR 2000 per month and base surplus is INR 5000.
Cash reserves are not confused with total net worth.
The target is justified for the invented household, not presented as personalized advice.

questions.prompt: Income is 40000 and monthly outflows including reserves are 35000. What is the surplus?
questions.explanation: 40000 minus 35000 is 5000. Ignoring periodic bills would overstate spendable surplus.

questions.prompt: Why can a household with positive net worth still miss a bill?
questions.answer: Its assets may be illiquid or unavailable when cash obligations fall due.
questions.explanation: Solvency and liquidity answer different questions; both matter in a financial plan.

reviewPrompts: Which irregular payment is easiest to overlook?

lessons.title: Compare debt by total cost and repayment behavior
objectives: Distinguish principal, interest, fees and repayment.
Explain nominal versus effective rates and the effects of missed or reduced payments.

topics.title: Borrowing arithmetic
details: Interest is charged on a stated balance under a stated convention.
Upfront fees can make equal quoted rates unequal in cost.

topics.title: Debt trade-offs
details: Minimum payments can extend repayment substantially.
A lower instalment may come from a longer term rather than a cheaper loan.

reading.locator: FAME Financial Competencies and Basic Banking themes: responsible borrowing, understanding terms and repayment. Read the terms of the invented exercise rather than assuming a current legal APR definition.

assignment.title: A two-offer debt comparison
instructions: Compare invented one-year loans of INR 12000: offer A has 1% monthly interest on the remaining balance with equal principal repayments; offer B has 10% flat annual interest plus a fee of INR 600.
Build the cash-flow schedule for both and state how upfront fees affect usable proceeds.
Explain the effect of one skipped principal payment under an explicitly invented no-penalty case; do not use real borrower data.
acceptanceCriteria: Offer A's interest uses a declining balance rather than the initial balance every month.
Fees and timing are included in the comparison.
A quoted lower percentage is not automatically labelled cheaper.

questions.prompt: What is one month's interest at 1% on a remaining principal of INR 12000?
questions.explanation: 12000 times 0.01 equals 120. Later interest depends on the remaining principal and the loan's stated convention.

questions.prompt: A smaller monthly instalment necessarily means what?
choices: Nothing about total cost without rate, fee and term information
A lower total borrowing cost
No interest is charged
questions.answer: Nothing about total cost without rate, fee and term information
questions.explanation: Extending the term can reduce each payment while increasing total interest. Compare cash flows, not one number.

reviewPrompts: What does the lender's quoted rate leave out?

modules.title: 02. Insurance, consumer protection and information hygiene
modules.description: Understand risk transfer, contract limits and authoritative sources before choosing products.

lessons.title: Explain insurance pooling, exclusions and retained risk
objectives: Separate insurable loss, premium, deductible and claim limit.
Compare protection needs without recommending a specific policy.

topics.title: Risk transfer
details: Pooling spreads uncertain covered losses across a group.
Insurance does not remove exclusions, deductibles or claims conditions.

topics.title: Protection choices
details: Health, life, disability and property cover respond to different losses.
Emergency liquidity and insurance complement rather than replace one another.

reading.locator: Chapter 1 Introduction, especially 1.2 A game of cat and mouse: read policy conditions and exclusions critically. Chapter 2 Perverse Incentives provides a commercial-incentive discussion.

assignment.title: An invented policy claims worksheet
instructions: Create a fictional policy with an INR 10000 deductible and INR 90000 maximum insurer payout; no coinsurance or other limits for this exercise.
Evaluate covered losses of 5000, 50000 and 150000, then a separately excluded loss.
Map the household's income/dependant/property risks to coverage questions and residual cash needs, without naming providers.
acceptanceCriteria: A covered INR 50000 loss produces insurer payout INR 40000 under the invented terms.
The 150000 case retains INR 60000 because the insurer payout is capped at 90000.
Excluded losses and claim documentation requirements remain explicit.

questions.prompt: A covered INR 50000 loss has a 10000 deductible and a non-binding payout cap. What does the insurer pay?
questions.explanation: 50000 minus the deductible 10000 equals 40000 under the exercise's simplified terms. Real contracts may have additional conditions.

questions.prompt: Why should policy premium not be the only comparison criterion?
questions.answer: Coverage, exclusions, waiting periods, limits, deductibles, claim process and the household's actual risks determine the protection provided.
questions.explanation: A cheaper contract may transfer less of the relevant risk; no particular product is recommended here.

reviewPrompts: What loss remains with the household even after a valid claim?

lessons.title: Verify financial claims and protect sensitive information
objectives: Identify authority, incentives and dates in financial information.
Recognize fraud signals and distinguish complaint routes from promises of recovery.

topics.title: Source checking
details: Registration is checked through official sources, not a promotional badge.
A source can be authoritative but outdated or outside the jurisdiction.

topics.title: Consumer protection
details: Never share passwords, OTPs or remote access for a supposed refund.
Keep minimal records and use official grievance channels.

reading.locator: Safeguarding against Securities Market Frauds and Investor Grievance Redress Mechanism; compare with FAME's Digital Financial Literacy and Consumer Protection themes.

assignment.title: A synthetic claim-verification log
instructions: Evaluate four invented messages: guaranteed returns, urgency to share an OTP, a dated regulatory statistic and a legitimate-looking but unverified registration claim.
For each, record the missing evidence and the official authority you would consult without contacting the sender.
Write a minimal incident record containing no real account numbers, identity documents or credentials.
acceptanceCriteria: No credential entry, transfer or contact with a suspicious party is performed.
Dates and jurisdiction are checked separately from branding.
Complaint channels are not represented as guaranteed recovery.

questions.prompt: A message asks for an OTP to release a refund. What is the appropriate learning response?
choices: Share it if a logo looks genuine
Do not share it; verify independently through an official channel
Publish it in the evidence log
questions.answer: Do not share it; verify independently through an official channel
questions.explanation: Logos and urgency do not establish authority. Authentication secrets should never be supplied to an unverified requester or included in learning artifacts.

questions.prompt: Why can a true US account rule be inappropriate in an Indian financial plan?
questions.answer: Legal scope and eligible products differ by jurisdiction, so a source must be relevant as well as accurate and current.
questions.explanation: Global materials teach concepts; Indian rules must be verified with the relevant Indian authority.

reviewPrompts: What independently verifiable evidence supports the claim?

modules.title: 03. Time value, inflation and financial goals
modules.description: Make cash-flow timing and purchasing-power assumptions explicit.

lessons.title: Discount cash flows and distinguish real from nominal value
objectives: Calculate present and future value for a single cash flow.
Match inflation-adjusted cash flows with consistent discount rates.

topics.title: Time value
details: Compounding moves value forward; discounting moves it backward.
Rate frequency and cash-flow timing must agree.

topics.title: Purchasing power
details: A nominal gain can be a real loss after inflation.
Nominal and real values cannot be mixed without conversion.

video.locator: Present Value Relations topic: single cash-flow discounting and compounding; use only the exercise's invented rates.

reading.locator: Section 7.3 Methods for Solving Time Value of Money Problems. Match the cash-flow date and periodic rate before calculating.

assignment.title: A purchasing-power timeline
instructions: Discount a fictional INR 1100 receipt in one year at an assumed 10% annual rate.
Compare a 6% nominal increase with 4% assumed inflation using both the exact ratio and a labelled approximation.
Show the same future goal in nominal and today's-money terms without claiming either assumed rate is current.
acceptanceCriteria: The INR 1100 receipt has present value INR 1000 at the assumed rate.
Exact real growth uses 1.06 divided by 1.04 minus 1.
All rates are explicitly hypothetical and use compatible periods.

questions.prompt: What is the present value of 1100 received in one year at a 10% assumed discount rate?
questions.explanation: 1100 divided by 1.10 equals 1000. This is a valuation under an assumption, not a market quote.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is internally consistent?
choices: Nominal cash flows with a nominal discount rate
Real cash flows with an unadjusted nominal rate
Monthly cash flows with an annual rate applied each month
questions.answer: Nominal cash flows with a nominal discount rate
questions.explanation: Both inflation treatment and time period must match. Inconsistent pairs distort value.

reviewPrompts: In which year's purchasing power is each number stated?

lessons.title: Model recurring payments and an amortizing loan
objectives: Build a payment schedule from interest and principal identities.
Explain how timing and term change total cost.

topics.title: Annuities
details: Beginning-period and end-period payments have different values.
A spreadsheet formula is only correct under its timing assumptions.

topics.title: Amortization
details: Payment equals interest plus principal reduction.
The final balance is a useful model invariant.

video.locator: Present Value Relations: multiple cash flows and annuities; verify end-of-period versus beginning-of-period timing.

reading.locator: Chapter 9 Debt Schedule: distinguish opening balance, interest, borrowing, repayment and closing balance. Build an original simplified household schedule.

assignment.title: A loan schedule with a zero-balance check
instructions: Use a fictional INR 12000 loan repaid in twelve end-of-month equal-principal instalments with 1% monthly interest.
Calculate each opening balance, interest, principal payment, total payment and closing balance.
Compare with a zero-interest case and a longer term; keep rounding differences visible and check the terminal balance.
acceptanceCriteria: Principal repayments sum to INR 12000.
First payment is INR 1120 and final payment INR 1010 before any invented fee.
The final principal balance is zero within a stated rounding tolerance.

questions.prompt: Opening principal is 3000, monthly rate 1% and principal repayment 1000. What is that month's total payment?
questions.explanation: Interest is 30 and principal reduction is 1000, producing a total payment of 1030.

questions.prompt: Why test a zero-interest case?
questions.answer: It provides a simple boundary where total payments should equal principal, helping expose formula, timing or sign errors.
questions.explanation: A hand-checkable boundary is a model audit tool, not just an alternative financial scenario.

reviewPrompts: Does each payment reconcile to interest plus principal?

lessons.title: Connect goals, protection and an income shock
objectives: Prioritize competing fictional goals by timing and liquidity needs.
Stress a household plan without assuming future returns will repair a deficit.

topics.title: Goal planning
details: Near-term essential spending and distant discretionary goals have different risk capacity.
Assumptions need periodic review rather than a one-time forecast.

topics.title: Resilience trade-offs
details: Debt service, premiums and cash buffers compete for a finite surplus.
A deficit must be addressed through explicit changes, not a promised investment gain.

reading.locator: Financial Planning Guide and Financial Education Booklet, English editions: organize goals and risk considerations; disregard any stale product/tax numbers unless currently verified.

assignment.title: Beginner evidence gate: a resilient fictional household
instructions: Combine l01 cash flows, l03 coverage assumptions and l06 debt schedule with a one-year essential goal and a five-year discretionary goal.
Stress three months without income, higher essential costs and an excluded claim.
Propose transparent changes to timing, spending or borrowing and record which goals are deferred; use no actual person's financial data.
acceptanceCriteria: The base plan and shock plan reconcile each month's cash.
At least one trade-off or unmet goal is explicitly recorded.
No speculative return, product recommendation or current-tax assertion is used to close a gap.

questions.prompt: A stress scenario creates a cash deficit. Which response is analytically honest?
choices: Assume a guaranteed high return
State a spending, timing or funding change and its consequences
Hide the deficit in miscellaneous assets
questions.answer: State a spending, timing or funding change and its consequences
questions.explanation: A model must expose trade-offs. Unfounded returns or balancing entries conceal the actual constraint.

questions.prompt: Why does a near-term essential goal limit capacity for volatile assets?
questions.answer: The spending date may arrive during a drawdown, leaving insufficient liquid funds even if long-term expected returns are positive.
questions.explanation: Horizon, liquidity and consequence of shortfall matter alongside expected return.

reviewPrompts: Which goal changes first if the assumptions fail?

modules.title: 04. Accounting and linked financial statements
modules.description: Explain accrual, balance-sheet claims and the movement of cash.

lessons.title: Translate business transactions into linked statements
objectives: Use the accounting equation to classify transactions.
Distinguish revenue recognition, cash receipt and financing.

topics.title: Accounting structure
details: Assets equal liabilities plus equity.
Every transaction has offsetting effects; profit changes equity but is not all cash.

topics.title: Accrual
details: Credit sales create receivables before collection.
Equipment purchase and depreciation have different cash and profit timing.

video.locator: Valuation Tools: From financial disclosures to value. Focus on locating statement inputs, not on the historical P&G valuation.

reading.locator: Chapters 4-5 Understanding the P&L Statement and 6-7 Understanding the Balance Sheet Statement. Trace the relationship between flows and closing balances.

assignment.title: Six transactions, three statements
instructions: Create a fictional firm: owner contributes 1000 cash, borrows 500, buys equipment for 600 cash, sells services for 400 on credit, pays wages 100 and records depreciation 60.
Prepare a transaction table, income statement and balance sheet; assume no taxes for this exercise.
Explain why profit and closing cash differ and retain the accounts-receivable balance.
acceptanceCriteria: Profit is 240 and cash is 800 under the specified assumptions.
Closing assets 1740 equal liabilities 500 plus equity 1240.
Borrowing is not revenue and equipment cost is not expensed twice.

questions.prompt: Revenue is 400, wages 100 and depreciation 60 with no tax. What is profit?
questions.explanation: 400 minus 100 minus 60 equals 240. Cash receipt timing does not change this simplified accrual calculation.

questions.prompt: Why is a new loan not operating revenue?
questions.answer: It creates cash and a repayment liability rather than income from delivering goods or services.
questions.explanation: Financing changes the capital structure; treating it as revenue overstates performance.

reviewPrompts: Which transaction changes cash without changing current profit?

lessons.title: Explain cash conversion and working-capital needs
objectives: Reconcile operating profit to cash with receivables, inventory and payables.
Show how growth can consume cash even when profitable.

topics.title: Cash-flow classification
details: Operating, investing and financing flows answer different questions.
Noncash expenses require reconciliation rather than a second cash deduction.

topics.title: Working capital
details: Receivables and inventory can absorb cash before customers pay.
Supplier credit can help temporarily but carries contractual obligations.

reading.locator: Chapter 8 The Cash Flow statement; use the operating/investing/financing distinction and reconcile noncash changes.

assignment.title: A profitable but cash-constrained company
instructions: Use profit 200, depreciation 40, receivables increase 150, inventory increase 100 and payables increase 30.
Build an indirect operating-cash bridge, then add capex 120 and financing 80.
Stress a further 60 delay in collections and state the funding shortfall without inventing sales.
acceptanceCriteria: Base operating cash flow is 20.
Capex and financing are not hidden inside operating profit.
The collection delay reduces cash by 60 while leaving the assumed accrual revenue unchanged.

questions.prompt: Using 200 profit + 40 depreciation - 150 receivables - 100 inventory + 30 payables, what is operating cash flow?
questions.explanation: The bridge yields 20. Positive profit can coexist with weak cash generation when working capital expands.

questions.prompt: Why is rapid sales growth not automatically self-financing?
questions.answer: Inventory, credit sales and operating capacity may need funding before cash is collected.
questions.explanation: The timing and working-capital intensity of growth determine its cash requirements.

reviewPrompts: Which balance-sheet account explains the largest profit/cash difference?

modules.title: 05. Ratios, comparability and earnings quality
modules.description: Use financial measures as questions to investigate, not mechanical verdicts.

lessons.title: Interpret margins, returns and solvency in context
objectives: Compute common-size statements and consistently defined ratios.
Compare businesses only after checking denominator, period and business-model differences.

topics.title: Measurement
details: Margins, turnover and leverage explain different drivers.
Average versus ending balance choices affect return measures.

topics.title: Comparability
details: Negative or near-zero denominators can make ratios misleading.
Sector, accounting policy and seasonality affect comparisons.

video.locator: Valuation Tools: ROIC and ROE: The "only" valuation numbers that matters. Critique denominator definitions and historical example assumptions.

reading.locator: Chapters 9-11 The Financial Ratio Analysis. State each numerator, denominator and averaging convention explicitly.

assignment.title: A two-firm ratio comparison with caveats
instructions: Invent two small firms with the same sales but different margins, assets and debt; keep statements balanced.
Compute operating margin, current ratio, debt/equity and return on average assets with defined periods.
Add a negative-equity case and explain why a mechanical ranking breaks.
acceptanceCriteria: All formulas disclose the relevant period and balance convention.
A near-zero or negative denominator is flagged rather than used for a confident ranking.
At least one business-model explanation is separated from the arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Operating profit 120 on revenue 1000 gives what operating margin in percent?
questions.explanation: 120 divided by 1000 times 100 is 12%. The number still needs context about costs, accounting and business model.

questions.prompt: Why can return on ending assets differ from return on average assets?
questions.answer: Assets may change during the earning period, so the ending snapshot may not represent the capital used throughout that period.
questions.explanation: Flow measures should be paired with a defensible stock denominator.

reviewPrompts: Which ranking changes when you correct the denominator?

lessons.title: Investigate one-offs, estimates and cash reconciliation
objectives: Distinguish recurring operations from disclosed unusual items.
Create an evidence trail for normalized figures without accusing real firms.

topics.title: Earnings quality
details: Accounting estimates and revenue timing affect reported results.
An adjustment is a judgment that needs evidence and consistent treatment.

topics.title: Audit mindset
details: Footnotes and reconciliations can explain apparent anomalies.
Analytical red flags are not proof of wrongdoing.

video.locator: Valuation Tools: Creating a trailing 12-month financial statement. Identify period overlap and avoid double counting historical quarters.

reading.locator: Chapter 3 How to Read the Annual Report of a Company and Chapter 12 The Investment Due Diligence. Trace each adjustment to a stated fictional note.

assignment.title: A normalized-profit evidence bridge
instructions: Invent reported operating profit 300 including a disclosed one-time asset gain of 80 and restructuring expense of 30.
Show reported versus adjusted profit under two defensible treatments of the restructuring cost.
Add rising receivables and a revenue-recognition note; state follow-up questions rather than a fraud accusation.
acceptanceCriteria: Removing the gain gives 220; also adding back the expense gives 250, with a reason for either treatment.
Reported and adjusted numbers are both retained.
Judgments and unverified concerns are labelled as such.

questions.prompt: Reported operating profit 300 contains a nonrecurring gain of 80. Removing only that gain yields what?
questions.explanation: 300 minus 80 equals 220. Additional adjustments require separate justification rather than selective optimism.

questions.prompt: Why should both reported and normalized figures remain visible?
questions.answer: A reader must be able to inspect the original result, reproduce each adjustment and disagree with the analyst's judgment.
questions.explanation: Transparency matters more than presenting a single seemingly precise corrected number.

reviewPrompts: Would you apply the same adjustment if it made results worse?

modules.title: 06. Investments, diversification and policy
modules.description: Compare cash-flow claims and construct a hypothetical policy, never a recommendation for the learner's money.

lessons.title: Compare asset claims and interest-rate sensitivity
objectives: Explain equity, debt, pooled funds and cash by claims and risks.
Price a simple bond and reason about rate/default risk.

topics.title: Claims and horizons
details: Contractual payments can still default.
Liquidity and inflation risk differ from price volatility.

topics.title: Bond valuation
details: Discount coupons and principal at consistent rates.
Longer-duration cash flows are generally more rate sensitive, all else equal.

video.locator: Present Value Relations: discount multiple cash flows, then apply the method to a fictional bond.

reading.locator: Section 10.1 Characteristics of Bonds and Section 7.3 Methods for Solving Time Value of Money Problems. Use fictional terms, not current yields.

assignment.title: A bond and asset-risk comparison
instructions: Price a one-year fictional bond paying 50 coupon plus 1000 principal at assumed required returns of 5% and 10%.
Compare its liquidity, default and inflation risks with cash, an equity claim and a diversified fund.
Add a missed-payment scenario; do not treat a coupon promise as a guarantee.
acceptanceCriteria: At 5% the bond value is 1000; at 10% it is about 954.55.
A higher discount rate reduces value for the same promised cash flow.
Default and liquidity risks are not erased by the valuation formula.

questions.prompt: A one-year bond pays 1050 and is discounted at 5%. What is its value?
questions.explanation: 1050 divided by 1.05 equals 1000, assuming the promised payment is received.

questions.prompt: Why can a bond lose market value before maturity even if payments remain on schedule?
questions.answer: Required yields can rise or credit/liquidity risk can change, reducing the present value of unchanged promised payments.
questions.explanation: Payment performance and current market valuation are related but distinct.

reviewPrompts: Which risk is omitted by the simple discount-rate calculation?

lessons.title: Look through funds to holdings, costs and overlap
objectives: Explain how pooled funds, NAV and expenses work.
Assess diversification by underlying exposures rather than product count.

topics.title: Fund mechanics
details: A fund share represents pooled assets net of liabilities.
Expense ratios, tracking differences and transaction costs affect realized outcomes.

topics.title: Diversification
details: Two funds may own largely the same assets.
Diversification reduces some idiosyncratic risk, not every market loss.

reading.locator: Introduction to Mutual Funds Investing; Introduction to Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs); Mutual Funds for Beginners. Use the official educational explanations, not current product recommendations.

assignment.title: A two-fund overlap and fee worksheet
instructions: Invent two funds with disclosed weights across four fictional assets and calculate the combined look-through allocation.
Compare an assumed 6% gross annual return with 0.5% and 1.5% annual cost under a clearly stated simplified subtraction convention.
Discuss tracking, liquidity and shared-factor risks; no real fund is selected.
acceptanceCriteria: Combined asset weights sum to 100%.
The report identifies overlap rather than counting funds as independent exposures.
Assumed gross returns and simplified fee timing are labelled, not promised.

questions.prompt: Half the portfolio is in Fund A with 60% Asset X and half in Fund B with 20% Asset X. What percent of the total is X?
questions.explanation: 0.5 times 60% plus 0.5 times 20% equals 40%. Product count alone would conceal this exposure.

questions.prompt: Why might two broad-looking funds provide little additional diversification?
questions.answer: Their underlying holdings or economic risk factors can overlap substantially.
questions.explanation: Look through wrappers to the actual exposures and how they may move together.

reviewPrompts: Which costs are visible in a stated expense ratio, and which are not?

lessons.title: Write a fictional investment policy and rebalance rule
objectives: Translate horizon, liquidity and loss capacity into constraints.
Design a rule-based, cost-aware review process without market timing promises.

topics.title: Policy design
details: Goals, constraints and governance precede asset selection.
Risk willingness and financial ability to bear loss may differ.

topics.title: Rebalancing
details: Bands or calendar reviews trade target adherence against turnover.
A policy can require holding cash for near-term obligations.

reading.locator: Financial Planning Guide and Mutual Funds for Intermediate: connect horizon, risk and diversification, while leaving all personal product decisions outside this exercise.

assignment.title: Intermediate evidence gate: a constrained policy
instructions: Use the fictional household, preserving its emergency cash and debt obligations.
Specify a hypothetical allocation, liquidity floor, review frequency, rebalance bands and maximum permitted transaction budget.
Apply an invented market decline and an approaching goal date; reconcile proposed changes and identify when abstaining from a rebalance is justified.
acceptanceCriteria: No essential near-term payment depends on an assumed market gain.
The policy states who reviews changes and what triggers reconsideration.
Rebalancing respects costs, cash needs and the documented hypothetical constraints.

questions.prompt: What should guide a hypothetical allocation before choosing products?
choices: The highest recent return alone
Goals, time horizon, liquidity and ability to bear loss
A guarantee that diversification prevents losses
questions.answer: Goals, time horizon, liquidity and ability to bear loss
questions.explanation: A defensible policy starts with constraints and purpose. Recent performance or false safety claims cannot replace them.

questions.prompt: Why can a fixed rebalance rule still need governance?
questions.answer: Goals, liquidity needs, costs or assumptions can change, and exceptions must be reviewed and documented rather than improvised.
questions.explanation: A rule is part of a decision process, not permission to ignore changed circumstances.

reviewPrompts: Which constraint takes priority over returning to target weights?

modules.title: 07. Capital budgeting and financing
modules.description: Evaluate incremental cash flows and the cost of financing under uncertainty.

lessons.title: Evaluate an incremental project with NPV
objectives: Separate sunk, incremental and opportunity costs.
Compare NPV with payback and explain decision conflicts.

topics.title: Cash-flow scope
details: Include working capital, replacement effects and terminal cash flows when relevant.
Exclude sunk costs from a forward incremental decision.

topics.title: Decision measures
details: Discounting accounts for timing and a stated required return.
IRR and payback can misrank projects of different scale or cash-flow pattern.

video.locator: Present Value Relations: multiple-date discounting; apply the method to incremental project cash flows.

reading.locator: Chapters 6 Revenue model, 7-8 Asset Schedule and 15 Valuation (Part 2) - FCFF & FCFE. Distinguish operating investment from financing flows.

assignment.title: An incremental equipment decision
instructions: Evaluate a fictional outlay of 1000 now and cash receipts 600 at the end of each of two years at an assumed 10% required return.
Add a previously spent research cost of 100 and explain why it is not a new outlay in the decision.
Stress operating receipts and working-capital recovery; compare NPV with undiscounted payback.
deliverables: NPV sensitivity and recommendation for the fictional firm only
acceptanceCriteria: Base NPV is approximately 41.32, with formulas visible.
The sunk research cost is separated from future incremental cash flows.
The decision changes or is qualified when scenario assumptions weaken.

questions.prompt: Compute -1000 + 600/1.1 + 600/1.1^2, rounded to two decimals.
questions.explanation: Discounted receipts total about 1041.32, leaving NPV 41.32. This small positive result depends on the assumed cash flows and discount rate.

questions.prompt: Why can a short payback period disagree with an NPV ranking?
questions.answer: Payback can ignore timing within the period and cash flows after the recovery point, while NPV includes discounted incremental cash flows over the horizon.
questions.explanation: Measures answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable.

reviewPrompts: Which cash flow disappears if the project is not undertaken?

lessons.title: Match financing risk and discount rates
objectives: Distinguish debt cost, equity cost and weighted capital cost.
Explain leverage benefits, distress costs and cash-flow/rate consistency.

topics.title: Financing
details: Debt creates contractual obligations; equity bears residual risk.
More leverage can raise distress risk and the required return on equity.

topics.title: WACC
details: Use consistent weights, currency and tax assumptions.
Do not discount equity cash flow at an enterprise cash-flow rate.

reading.locator: Chapters 15 FCFF & FCFE, 16 Risk Premium & Tax Shield and 17 Weighted average cost of capital and Terminal Growth. Treat any tax rate in the reading as an example, not current Indian law.

assignment.title: A financing and discount-rate consistency sheet
instructions: Use fictional weights of 60% equity and 40% debt, equity cost 12%, debt cost 8% and an explicitly assumed 25% tax rate used only for arithmetic.
Calculate after-tax WACC and compare an alternative with greater debt and a higher equity/debt risk premium.
Map enterprise cash flows to WACC and equity cash flows to cost of equity, noting where tax-shield availability is uncertain.
acceptanceCriteria: Base WACC is 9.6% under the invented assumptions.
The assumed tax input is not described as a prevailing tax rate.
No claim is made that increasing leverage always lowers total financing cost.

questions.prompt: What is 0.6*12% + 0.4*8%*(1-0.25), expressed as a percent?
questions.explanation: The weighted equity cost is 7.2% and weighted after-tax debt cost is 2.4%, totaling 9.6% under these fictional assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why does more debt not guarantee a lower WACC?
questions.answer: Lenders and shareholders can demand higher returns as distress and refinancing risks rise, and tax benefits may be limited or unavailable.
questions.explanation: Capital costs respond to risk; holding them fixed while changing leverage can produce a misleading result.

reviewPrompts: Do the cash flow, currency and discount rate belong to the same claim?

modules.title: 08. Valuation ranges and macroeconomic context
modules.description: Use multiple methods and current-source discipline to explain a range rather than manufacture a target price.

lessons.title: Build a DCF and challenge terminal value
objectives: Discount explicit forecast cash flows and a consistent terminal value.
Expose sensitivity to growth, margins, reinvestment and discount rates.

topics.title: Value drivers
details: Growth usually needs reinvestment and cannot be free by assumption.
Terminal assumptions can dominate a short explicit forecast.

topics.title: Model boundaries
details: A perpetual-growth denominator requires discount rate greater than growth.
A scenario range is not a guaranteed trading price.

video.locator: Valuation Tools: Terminal Value Check. Audit the long-run assumptions rather than copying the historical spreadsheet.

reading.locator: Chapters 17 Weighted average cost of capital and Terminal Growth and 18 Discounted Cash Flow Analysis (DCF). Explain the terminal cash-flow timing and reinvestment assumptions.

assignment.title: A terminal-value-sensitive fictional business
instructions: Forecast three years of original synthetic operating cash flows with explicit capex and working-capital assumptions.
Compute terminal value using next-period cash flow 105, assumed discount rate 10% and perpetual growth 5%, then discount it from the terminal date.
Create a rate/growth sensitivity grid including invalid cases where growth meets or exceeds the discount rate.
acceptanceCriteria: Undiscounted terminal value is 2100 under the given terminal inputs.
The terminal amount is discounted to the valuation date exactly once.
Invalid perpetual-growth combinations produce a visible error, not a plausible value.

questions.prompt: Next-period terminal cash flow is 105, discount rate 10% and growth 5%. What is terminal value at the terminal date?
questions.explanation: 105 divided by (0.10 minus 0.05) is 2100. It still needs discounting back to the valuation date.

questions.prompt: Why is a perpetual growth rate near the discount rate dangerous in a model?
questions.answer: The denominator becomes very small, making value extremely sensitive and potentially inconsistent with sustainable long-run economics.
questions.explanation: A mathematically large value can be a sign of fragile assumptions rather than a valuable business.

reviewPrompts: How much of the valuation depends on the least observable assumption?

lessons.title: Reconcile enterprise, firm and equity values
objectives: Build an enterprise-to-equity bridge with consistent claims.
Use comparable multiples while checking operating and accounting differences.

topics.title: Value bridge
details: Operating asset value differs from equity value after debt and other claims.
Cash, non-operating assets and diluted shares need consistent treatment.

topics.title: Comparables
details: A multiple must match the numerator's claim to the denominator's flow.
Growth, profitability, leverage and one-offs affect comparability.

video.locator: Valuation Tools: EV, Firm Value and Equity Value; Multiples and Fundamentals - Analyzing relationships. Distinguish operating and equity claims.

reading.locator: Chapter 14 Valuation (Part 1) - Overview and Chapter 15 FCFF & FCFE; compare what is being valued before applying a multiple.

assignment.title: A value bridge and imperfect peer set
instructions: Use fictional enterprise value 2000, debt 600, surplus cash 150 and no other claims; calculate equity value and value per 100 diluted shares.
Create three fictional peers with different margins, growth and debt; compare an enterprise multiple and an equity multiple.
Document one peer exclusion and one alternative treatment that changes the range.
acceptanceCriteria: Equity value is 1550 and per-share value is 15.5 under the simplified assumptions.
Enterprise and equity multiples use compatible denominators.
The peer range is not presented as a buy/sell recommendation.

questions.prompt: Enterprise value 2000 minus debt 600 plus surplus cash 150 gives what equity value?
questions.explanation: 2000 - 600 + 150 = 1550 before any other claims or adjustments.

questions.prompt: Why can comparing enterprise value to net income be inconsistent?
questions.answer: Enterprise value covers operating claims before financing, while net income is after interest and belongs to equity under the usual definitions.
questions.explanation: Numerator and denominator must refer to compatible claimholders.

reviewPrompts: Which claim or non-operating asset is missing from the bridge?

lessons.title: Trace macroeconomic and institutional transmission
objectives: Explain how policy rates, credit conditions, inflation and exchange rates can affect cash flows.
Distinguish central-bank, market-regulator and fiscal roles.

topics.title: Institutions
details: Monetary policy, fiscal policy and securities regulation have different responsibilities.
Policy announcements do not mechanically determine every retail borrowing or market rate.

topics.title: Scenario channels
details: Currency movements can affect imported costs, export revenue and foreign debt differently.
Demand, margin and discount-rate effects can offset or amplify each other.

reading.locator: Select English in Money Kumar, the RBI series explaining the Reserve Bank's roles and functions. Pair institutional concepts with the SEBI investor material; do not use the booklet for current policy rates.

assignment.title: Advanced evidence gate: macro-to-value scenario map
instructions: Use the fictional business from l17 with some imported inputs and one foreign-currency borrowing exposure.
Create rate-rise, currency-depreciation and demand-slowdown scenarios; trace each through operating cash, financing and valuation separately.
Link the NPV decision, value bridge and official-source register, using invented shocks rather than asserting a live macro forecast.
deliverables: Causal channel map and revised valuation ranges
acceptanceCriteria: At least one scenario has competing positive and negative channels.
No current policy, exchange, tax or regulatory number is asserted without a dated official source.
The scenario is labelled conditional analysis, not a forecast or trading instruction.

questions.prompt: For a firm importing inputs and earning only domestic revenue, local currency depreciation may directly do what?
choices: Raise local-currency input costs, other things equal
Leave domestic input costs unchanged because invoice currency is unchanged
Lower domestic input costs because the local currency lost purchasing power
questions.answer: Raise local-currency input costs, other things equal
questions.explanation: The foreign-currency purchase price translates into more domestic currency. Pricing power, hedges and other exposures can modify the total effect.

questions.prompt: Why separate operating and discount-rate effects in a scenario?
questions.answer: A shock can change both expected cash flows and required returns; separating channels makes assumptions auditable and avoids hidden double counting.
questions.explanation: A single unexplained valuation adjustment obscures the mechanism.

reviewPrompts: Which institution has authority over the specific claim you are making?

modules.title: 09. Integrated modelling and independent audit
modules.description: Build schedules that reconcile and expose failure instead of plugging discrepancies.

lessons.title: Link operating, asset, debt and cash schedules
objectives: Forecast a small three-statement model from explicit business drivers.
Keep financing shortfalls visible instead of adding unexplained balancing plugs.

topics.title: Model architecture
details: Separate assumptions, historical inputs, schedules and outputs.
Revenue, working capital, capex, depreciation and debt must agree across statements.

topics.title: Reconciliation
details: Closing cash follows the cash-flow statement.
Retained earnings follow profit and distributions; unexplained differences are errors.

video.locator: Valuation Tools: From financial disclosures to value; use the extraction workflow, but create original synthetic inputs rather than copying the historical company workbook.

reading.locator: Chapters 2 Excel workbook setup, 4-5 Assumptions, 6 Revenue model, 7-9 Asset and Debt Schedules, 12 Projections and 13 Cash flow statement. Translate to free LibreOffice or Python.

assignment.title: A driver-based three-year model
instructions: Invent and balance an opening statement, then forecast three years using unit sales, unit price, cost margin, collection days and capex assumptions.
Link depreciation, debt interest, repayments, retained earnings and cash.
Run a downside case that creates a financing need; expose the deficit and a separately specified financing choice rather than hiding it.
acceptanceCriteria: Assets equal liabilities plus equity in each period.
Cash-flow closing cash equals balance-sheet cash.
Financing assumptions, circular dependencies and any unresolved deficit are explicit.

questions.prompt: An unexplained cash plug that makes the balance sheet balance is best treated as what?
choices: A valid funding source that need not appear in the financing schedule
An automatic reduction in working-capital investment
A model error or undisclosed financing assumption to investigate
questions.answer: A model error or undisclosed financing assumption to investigate
questions.explanation: Balancing mechanically does not explain where funds come from. Every cash change needs an economic source.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of driver-based revenue over typing a desired total?
questions.answer: Units, prices and capacity assumptions become inspectable and can be stressed independently, revealing the mechanism behind growth.
questions.explanation: A transparent causal model is easier to challenge than an unexplained output target.

reviewPrompts: Which schedule first reveals the downside funding need?

lessons.title: Audit units, formulas, scenarios and source lineage
objectives: Detect sign, timing, unit and formula-link errors.
Record review findings and corrections without overwriting prior evidence.

topics.title: Model checks
details: Test zeros, boundary rates and invalid terminal assumptions.
Separate hard-coded inputs from formulas and clearly label currency/unit scale.

topics.title: Review independence
details: A reviewer samples calculations and follows references to their sources.
A corrected version needs a traceable change log and regenerated outputs.

video.locator: Valuation Tools: Terminal Value Check; apply the same skeptical review to formula boundaries and sensitivity tables.

reading.locator: Chapter 2 Excel workbook setup and Chapter 3 Historical Data; inspect input/formula separation and source consistency in the original model you built.

assignment.title: A four-defect financial-model challenge
instructions: In copied synthetic workbooks, introduce a thousands-versus-units mismatch, a reversed working-capital sign, a broken formula reference and an invalid terminal growth rate.
Write checks that identify each defect and confirm the clean model still reconciles.
Record severity, affected decisions, fix and regenerated output under a new version.
deliverables: Audit checklist and four fault fixtures
acceptanceCriteria: All four inserted defects are caught by named checks.
The clean version passes balance, cash and timing checks.
Source/version changes remain visible; no false claim of independent certification is made.

questions.prompt: Which check is most useful for a thousands-versus-units error?
choices: Explicit unit labels and a dimensional consistency check
Checking balance-sheet equality alone even if both sides share a scale error
Comparing chart shapes without verifying currency and magnitude
questions.answer: Explicit unit labels and a dimensional consistency check
questions.explanation: The arithmetic can be internally precise while units are inconsistent. Labels and cross-checks expose the mismatch.

questions.prompt: Why keep an old model version after correcting an error?
questions.answer: It allows reviewers to understand which outputs and decisions changed and why, while the corrected version becomes the clearly identified current artifact.
questions.explanation: Auditability requires lineage, not preserving an error as if it were still valid.

reviewPrompts: Which wrong result would still look plausible without an invariant?

modules.title: 10. Financial-analysis capstone and decision governance
modules.description: Bring household constraints, business economics and model uncertainty into one accountable evidence dossier.

lessons.title: Write an assumption-led financial decision memo
objectives: Separate observed facts, fictional inputs, estimates and judgments.
Explain alternatives, conflicts and downside conditions to a non-specialist.

topics.title: Decision communication
details: Lead with the question, alternatives and constraints.
Show ranges and major drivers rather than false precision.

topics.title: Ethics and scope
details: Disclose commercial conflicts, missing data and jurisdiction limits.
An educational analysis is not personalized financial, tax or investment advice.

reading.locator: Financial Planning Guide and Safeguarding against Securities Market Frauds: review how claims, suitability and source authority should be communicated.

assignment.title: A two-page, bounded decision memo
instructions: Compare undertake, defer and reject for the fictional project using NPV, funding and downside evidence.
Label every key figure as synthetic input, derived result or external contextual fact with a dated source.
Include conflicts, limitations, a contrary interpretation and conditions for revisiting the decision.
acceptanceCriteria: The memo distinguishes model output from market fact.
It discusses an adverse case and a credible alternative.
No actual security, tax filing or financial product recommendation is issued.

questions.prompt: Which wording is defensible for an assumption-driven valuation?
choices: A point estimate accurate to two decimals regardless of assumption uncertainty
A value established solely by reusing last year's peer multiple
The model implies a range under these stated scenarios
questions.answer: The model implies a range under these stated scenarios
questions.explanation: A model is conditional reasoning. It does not compel market prices or remove uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Why state a contrary interpretation?
questions.answer: It exposes the judgments and assumptions that could change the decision and helps a reviewer avoid being led by a one-sided presentation.
questions.explanation: A useful memo supports scrutiny rather than merely defending its author's preferred conclusion.

reviewPrompts: Which uncertainty matters to the decision more than another decimal place?

lessons.title: Deliver an audited household and business analysis dossier
objectives: Integrate financial resilience, accounting and corporate valuation evidence.
Make every material conclusion reproducible and bounded by assumptions.

topics.title: Cross-scale reasoning
details: A household's liquidity constraints and a firm's funding constraints share timing concepts but not identical rules.
Investment analysis is distinct from advice to purchase an actual asset.

topics.title: Evidence gates
details: Models, sources and memo claims must reconcile.
A reviewer must reproduce both a base result and an adverse scenario.

reading.locator: Chapters 12-18 Projections, Cash flow statement and Valuation; revisit only the sections needed to justify your original integrated model.

assignment.title: Capstone: a reproducible financial decision dossier
instructions: Finalize a synthetic household cash/debt/insurance/goal plan and a separate synthetic company's three-statement forecast, NPV and valuation range.
Include a macro/working-capital downside, enterprise-to-equity bridge, model checks and an authority/date register for contextual claims.
Provide the input pack, formulas or code, audit trail and decision memo so another learner can regenerate results without paid software or personal data.
deliverables: Two clearly separated synthetic case input packs
Household resilience plan and integrated corporate model
Claim-linked memo, source register and reviewer instructions
acceptanceCriteria: Household cash, debt principal and coverage limits reconcile under a loss-of-income scenario.
Corporate statements, cash flow and debt/asset schedules reconcile for every forecast period.
Cash-flow types, rates, currency units and terminal assumptions are consistent.
A downside funding need is visible rather than solved by an unexplained plug.
No current tax/regulatory figure is fabricated or imported from another jurisdiction.
The reviewer can reproduce a base case, an adverse case and a planted error detection.
The dossier makes no certification, personal advice or guaranteed-return claim.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most strengthens this capstone?
choices: A precise point estimate with terminal assumptions chosen to match a target
A base case with balanced statements but no adverse funding analysis
Reproducible calculations and an openly explained downside
questions.answer: Reproducible calculations and an openly explained downside
questions.explanation: The assessment rewards reasoning, consistency and transparency, not a favorable result.

questions.prompt: Why keep household and business cases separate even when using shared finance concepts?
questions.answer: Their objectives, obligations, legal context and decision constraints differ; shared arithmetic does not make assumptions or advice interchangeable.
questions.explanation: Transfer concepts carefully while preserving the scope of each analysis.

reviewPrompts: Can the reviewer regenerate a conclusion from source inputs rather than trust a screenshot?

lessons.title: Defend the analysis and establish a review cadence
objectives: Respond to a skeptical financial-model review with evidence.
Define triggers for updating assumptions and retiring stale conclusions.

topics.title: Challenge and correction
details: A peer or delayed blind self-review selects calculations and scenarios.
Material errors require corrected outputs and a revised decision, not just a footnote.

topics.title: Ongoing governance
details: Assumptions have owners, dates and refresh triggers.
Professional Practice does not award a regulated qualification.

video.locator: Valuation Tools: Terminal Value Check and EV, Firm Value and Equity Value. Use these as a challenge checklist for your final model, not as an authority approving it.

reading.locator: General guidance and good practice for testing: Document the tests and how to run them; Reproducible Environments. Apply the evidence standard to the model handover.

assignment.title: A financial-analysis handover and challenge record
instructions: Ask a peer or delayed self-reviewer to select one household cash shock, one corporate bridge and one valuation assumption for independent recalculation.
Record disagreements, corrected versions and any remaining blockers to the decision.
Set review triggers for changed goals, funding terms, source currency or business drivers; retain a dated final limitations statement.
acceptanceCriteria: Reviewer-selected results are reproduced or marked unresolved.
Material corrections propagate to the memo and all dependent outputs.
Review triggers are event-based as well as calendar-based, with no qualification claim.

questions.prompt: A material debt-schedule error changes valuation. What needs revision?
choices: Only the debt tab because the summary is a separate presentation
The affected model outputs and decision memo
Only the written disclaimer without regenerating dependent outputs
questions.answer: The affected model outputs and decision memo
questions.explanation: A model supports decisions through linked calculations. Material changes must propagate through that chain.

questions.prompt: Give an event that should trigger review before the next scheduled date.
questions.answer: Examples include a lost income source, changed financing terms, a major business-model change or new authoritative information invalidating a material assumption.
questions.explanation: A calendar alone cannot keep a decision valid when its key conditions change.

reviewPrompts: Which assumption could make today's conclusion stale tomorrow?

sources.notes: Institution/product-neutral public education and exact official video link verified.

sources.title: SEBI financial planning and investor safeguards
sources.notes: Named English booklets available from the official index; no local redistribution.

sources.title: Varsity financial modelling chapter index
sources.notes: Free HTML; spreadsheet concepts transfer to LibreOffice or Python.

sources.title: NYU Stern valuation webcasts and model checks
sources.notes: Free author-hosted recordings; historical examples are not current accounting law or market data.

limitations: Finance assignments use fictional households and businesses, not real personal account data. They teach analysis, not personalized investment, insurance, borrowing or tax advice; no product purchase or guaranteed return is required.
Professional Practice describes a learning level, not a professional certification, qualification, regulated advisory status or independently verified competence.

All rates, premiums, tax assumptions and exchange-rate shocks in exercises are explicitly invented. Check current Indian rules with the relevant regulator; historical US examples do not establish Indian law.

The required route uses free official HTML/externally linked readings, free videos where relevant and LibreOffice or local Python. Paid textbooks, Microsoft Excel, subscriptions and certificates are unnecessary.
Readings remain at their official hosts. Do not copy or redistribute book chapters, recordings, company workbooks or third-party data without permission.
Shared finance, research and Common Foundation resources/lessons retain their canonical IDs. Optional topic progress does not replace or dilute core-path progress.
